_note: GENERATED by `go run ./scripts/evalindex`. The cards are authored; their claims about coverage are checked against the repository by the companion tests, because a registry free to say whatever it likes about how well kapi is measured would be the opposite of evidence.

bands.title: Engine and formats
bands.subject: kapi's own code: what it does to a document it reads, holds and writes back.
bands.evidence: Deterministic. The same document produces the same content model every run, so these evals assert rather than estimate, and a regression is a fact rather than a shift in a distribution.
bands.gates: Yes. A failure here stops a build.

bands.title: AI and context
bands.subject: What a model writes under kapi's governance, and whether the governance reached it.
bands.evidence: Sampled. A score is an estimate over a corpus, and where a model does the scoring it is an estimate of an estimate. Corpus size is the ceiling on what any of it can conclude, so every card states it.
bands.gates: No. These are tracked over time, and a drop is a signal to look rather than a build failure.

bands.title: Agent skills
bands.subject: An agent driving kapi: the shipped Agent Skill, and the MCP tools an assistant calls.
bands.evidence: Scenario-scored. A prompt and a workspace go in, and what the agent did comes out: which tool it reached for, whether it finished at a green gate. No model grades anything. Triggering is stochastic, so a scenario means little until it is repeated.
bands.gates: No, and these never run in CI. They drive an interactive agent on a maintainer's machine, so the committed dataset is all CI sees and the date on it is the real currency of the numbers.

layers.title: Foundations
layers.scope: The content model every format is read into, how a piece of content is identified, and the wire schema that carries it.

layers.title: Engine
layers.scope: Reading a format, running tools over the content, binding flows, and writing the document back unchanged where nothing was edited.
layers.rests: the content model being able to hold what the format carried

layers.title: Context
layers.scope: What governs content at the point it sits: the coordinates, the voice profile, the terms, and the content memory holding what was already approved.
layers.rests: the engine putting the right content in front of the governance

layers.title: Multilingual
layers.scope: The call itself: what goes into a prompt, how many blocks travel together, and how the text was split before any of that.
layers.rests: the context layer having resolved what applies before a prompt is built

layers.title: Assurance
layers.scope: The checks that read finished content and report what breaks the rules, and whether they are right about it.
layers.rests: every layer below, since a check reports on what they produced

layers.title: Surfaces
layers.scope: How kapi is reached: the CLI, the desktop app, the shipped Agent Skill, and the MCP tools an assistant calls.
layers.rests: every layer below, since a surface is how a person or an agent gets at them

evals.title: KBF conformance across engines
evals.corpus: The KBF conformance suite, run against the Go engine compiled to WebAssembly and the TypeScript mirror.
evals.covers: That two independent implementations of the bundle format agree, operation by operation, in your browser.
evals.misses: Runs only when someone opens the page. Nothing in CI executes it, so it reports rather than gates. The structural and envelope checks run on the Go engine alone, and identity (F-03) is not measured at all.

evals.title: Filter parity against upstream Okapi
evals.corpus: The Okapi Framework's own filter test suite, mapped onto neokapi's readers.
evals.covers: Whether a document read by neokapi produces the same content model as the Java implementation it descends from, per format.
evals.misses: Publishes nothing. The report lands in a gitignored sandbox and the dashboard that used to render it was retired, so the result is visible only to whoever ran it. Formats with no upstream counterpart are unmeasurable this way, and a known-failure list is carried rather than fixed.

evals.title: Format maturity, L0 to L4
evals.corpus: Every registered format, scored against a fixed rubric.
evals.covers: How far each format has been taken: read, write, round-trip, inline codes, faithful write-back.
evals.misses: A rubric level is a claim about capability, not about quality on your documents.

evals.title: Engine throughput
evals.corpus: 844 fixtures on the pseudo-translation path, which exercises read and write without a model, across four engines.
evals.covers: How fast each engine moves content when no provider is in the way, with the count of files whose output actually contains pseudo-translated text beside the timing, so an engine that is fast because it read less is visible as such.
evals.misses: Isolates the engine deliberately, so it says nothing about a run that calls a model. One machine, one platform.

evals.title: What a local model costs to run
evals.corpus: The bundled ML models, on one machine's runtime.
evals.covers: What a user pays in download size, cold start, per-sentence inference and resident memory.
evals.misses: Measured on one platform. A different runtime or accelerator moves every number.

evals.title: kapi against other converters
evals.corpus: Needs a document corpus and independent ground truth, meaning rendered pages rather than another tool's output.
evals.covers: Would measure conversion speed and fidelity against markitdown, pandoc, docling, unstructured and LibreOffice.
evals.misses: Not built here. A harness of this shape exists in the anydoc repository and already includes kapi in its speed tables; neokapi publishes nothing of its own.

evals.title: What an author's edit does to reuse
evals.corpus: One approved sentence pair, edited eleven ways; a three-sentence paragraph; five governance scenarios.
evals.covers: Which rules apply where, whether an edited source still gets its approved translation, whether a prior version is offered or withheld, and what reaches the prompt.
evals.misses: One language pair. The edit ladder is one sentence, chosen for length rather than sampled.

evals.title: Whether the prior version changes what the model writes
evals.corpus: Six wording cases with a control, plus a 20-block document in three batching arms.
evals.covers: Whether showing the model a block's previously approved translation keeps the approved wording, and what it costs in calls and tokens.
evals.misses: One model, one language pair, one direction. The judged half has no measured agreement with a person; only the deterministic consistency half should be relied on.
evals.settings: Temperature 0, pinned in the harness and recorded in the dataset. Max tokens follow the model's ceiling. No seed: the API exposes none.

evals.title: What context injection is worth
evals.corpus: A synthetic brand corpus with a fixed rubric, swept across models.
evals.covers: Whether a model given voice guidance and terminology produces output that needs less correction than one that is not.
evals.misses: Judge-to-human agreement is gated at 30 labelled items; the literature puts the useful floor at 100 to 200, and no sweep has cleared even the lower bar.
evals.settings: Temperature 0 on every swept model, pinned in the harness. The committed sweep predates the field that records it, so the dataset carries no temperature of its own until the next one. Max tokens follow each model's ceiling. No seed: the APIs expose none.

evals.title: Whether the voice guide steers writing or just improves it
evals.corpus: Six briefs about a synthesized product, each written twice by one model: once bare, once with `kapi voice guide` as the system turn. Both versions scored against the profile the guide came from and against a contrast profile that wants the opposite.
evals.covers: Whether the guide moves writing toward its own profile specifically. Any competent writing guidance raises any reasonable score, so the reference gain alone proves nothing; the measurement is the difference between the two gains. Guided writing gained 5.8 points against the reference profile and lost 6.7 against the contrast, an effect of 12.5.
evals.misses: Six documents on one model. Scoring is the offline check, which evaluates forbidden terms and prohibited patterns and not the declared fields — so the person and sentence-length instructions the model read are not in the score. Part of the contrast arm's drop is mechanical: the contrast profile forbids `you`, and the guide asks for second person.
evals.settings: Temperature 0, and the user turn is byte-identical across arms. The bare arm has no system turn at all rather than a placebo one.

evals.title: Whether an inferred voice profile is usable
evals.corpus: Built and ready: the corpus's on-profile half was written from a reference profile, so recovery is checkable field by field rather than by asking a judge. The comparison runs the moment there is a draft.
evals.covers: Would measure how much of the reference profile a draft recovers — each tone and style field, and how many of the forbidden terms.
evals.misses: `kapi exec voice-infer` writes nothing to stdout and exits 0 (#2225), and it has no other surface: there is no `kapi voice infer` subcommand. There is no draft to compare.
evals.settings: Whatever provider the run names, at temperature 0. Nothing is recorded because the tool returns nothing; the field will carry the real settings with the first draft it produces.

evals.title: What each call actually sends
evals.corpus: The prompts built for the reuse evals, captured as they went to the model.
evals.covers: That the voice guide, the terminology a call can use, and a block's prior version are in the prompt, and that the cache key moves with them.
evals.misses: Reads the prompt kapi built, not the reply it got. It shows the governance arrived; whether the model followed it is context-value's question.

evals.title: What batching costs and saves
evals.corpus: 600 blocks swept across four batch sizes on two models, plus the earlier sweeps kept in the same history.
evals.covers: Throughput and structural integrity as blocks per call rises, priced per model. Both models hold every block to 128 per call and neither can answer at 600.
evals.misses: Concurrency is recorded because throughput depends on it, so two models swept at different concurrencies cannot be raced on speed. Segmentation (M-02) is not measured at all, and it decides what a block is before any of this runs.
evals.settings: Temperature 0, pinned in the harness. The committed sweep predates the field that records it, so the dataset carries concurrency but not temperature until the next one. No seed: the APIs expose none.

evals.title: Precision and recall of the content checks
evals.misses: Ten cases is too few to separate a real precision difference from noise. The voice checks are measured separately by authoring-checks; term-check is not measured by either, and belongs to neither — its examples are XLIFF with a target, so it scores translations against approved terms rather than source prose.

evals.title: Whether the voice checks find real violations
evals.corpus: Twelve synthesized documents about one product: six written to a voice profile, six written against it with 18 violations marked. The clean half is what makes false positives measurable.
evals.covers: Recall over the marked violations, split by how the profile expresses each rule. The offline check found 89% overall — every prohibited pattern, 12 of 13 forbidden terms, and none of the declared fields, which nothing offline evaluates. It also raised a finding on 3 of the 6 clean documents.
evals.misses: The LLM check cannot be scored: `kapi exec voice-check` returns nothing under every provider and profile tried (#2225). The one term miss is `utilizes` against a profile forbidding `utilize` (#2226). The corpus is synthesized, which is disclosed in the data itself.

evals.title: Whether the skill fires on the right tasks
evals.corpus: 17 prompts that must load the skill and 5 that must not, three passes each, every one in its own workspace holding the files the prompt names.
evals.covers: The only lever on triggering, which is the skill's description: does an assistant reach for kapi on a content task, and leave it alone on a code task. Activation counts a Skill call or a kapi command, so an agent that reads the skill once and then works from it is not scored as a miss.
evals.misses: Triggering only. A scenario that fires and then does the job badly passes here; whether the work is right is skill-completion's question. One model on one day, and the negatives are five prompts rather than a sample of the code tasks a real assistant sees.
evals.settings: claude -p with a 4-turn cap, bypassPermissions, 3 repeats. Sampling follows the local CLI's defaults and is not pinned.

evals.title: Whether the agent finishes the job
evals.corpus: 15 of the positive scenarios driven to the end in a sandboxed kapi with isolated config, data, cache and plugins.
evals.covers: That the agent does not merely start: it drives the loop to a green gate, with kapi check --ship or kapi check passing.
evals.misses: Scored at catalog-gate depth by decision, so in-locale rendering is never verified. Two scenarios are blocked on a private npm registry absent from the sandbox rather than on any skill defect.
evals.settings: claude -p in a sandboxed kapi, Gemini via env. Turn caps vary by scenario; sampling is not recorded.

evals.title: Whether an agent picks the right MCP tool
evals.corpus: Seven tasks with one right answer each among the nineteen tools the server advertises, plus one task no tool should answer. Three passes each.
evals.covers: The other door into kapi. An MCP client already holds the tool list, so it cannot fail to notice kapi; it fails by reaching for the wrong tool, and a near miss names two descriptions that are not telling each other apart.
evals.misses: Seven of nineteen tools have a scenario. The review and approval tools, redaction and translate are unmeasured. A wrong pick is recorded rather than diagnosed, and the negative is one prompt.
evals.settings: claude -p with --strict-mcp-config, so the run sees this checkout's server and nothing the developer has configured. Each scenario keeps its own turn budget, because picking a tool can take a step or two. Sampling is not pinned.
